passage: It was ten at night, the shops were shut, and tomorrow the family was coming for lunch. The kitchen cabinet door hung by one screw. Nilesh went to the shelf where his toolbox lived, with each tool in its place, and took out the right screwdriver, not the one that would nearly fit. He tightened the loose hinge screw, then wiped a drop of oil on the hinge so it would not squeak. His neighbour Jaya, who had come to borrow the drill, watched. "You always have everything." "I put it back after every job," he said. She left with the drill, and he wrote it in the book by the toolbox.

qa.a: The kitchen cabinet door hung by one screw.

qa.a: Nilesh is calm and settled, since he knows where each tool is and the job is small, even though the hour is late.

qa.a: He keeps tools in one place, uses the correct screwdriver and does small upkeep like oiling the hinge before it squeaks.

qa.a: Jaya is probably impressed and a little envious, since she says he always has everything.

passage: On Sunday mornings, Chetan gave his flat fifteen minutes. He took the toolbox from its shelf, where the labelled trays held screws by size, and tightened the wobbly chair leg with the right screwdriver. He cleaned the water filter, put a drop of oil on the door hinge and pumped up the tyre of his scooter. His sister Preeti, sitting with her tea, said, "You do this every week? For what?" "So it doesn't cost me more later," Chetan said. Three weeks later Preeti's landlord asked for a big bill for her cracked filter. Chetan's was still fine. She did not tease him again, and borrowed the screwdriver instead.

qa.q: How many minutes did Chetan give his flat on Sunday mornings?
qa.a: Chetan gave his flat fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What is Chetan feeling on Sunday mornings, judging from the answer to Preeti?
qa.a: Chetan seems calm and steady, treating small upkeep as cheap protection against bigger costs later.

qa.q: What habits kept Chetan's costs low?
qa.a: Chetan kept tools in labelled trays, used the right screwdriver and did small upkeep such as cleaning the filter and oiling the hinge before things failed.

qa.q: What changed for Preeti after her filter cracked?
qa.a: Preeti stopped teasing and borrowed the screwdriver instead, showing she could now see the value of small upkeep.

grounding: Shows a capable person keeping tools together, using the correct tool and doing small maintenance before things fail.

passage:
Reena: "Vishal, where's the screwdriver? The cupboard hinge is loose."
Vishal: "Blue box, bottom shelf. Everything's in there."
Reena: (opening it) "Wow. Labelled. Even the Allen keys."
Vishal: "I got tired of searching the whole flat every time."
Reena: "I usually just use a butter knife."
Vishal: "And that's why the screws in your kitchen are all chewed up."
Reena: "Fair. Which one for this?"
Vishal: "Cross-head, the medium one. The small one will strip it."
Reena: "What's this little oil can for?"
Vishal: "Door hinges and the cycle chain. First Sunday of every month. Takes ten minutes. Saves me buying a new chain every year."
Reena: "You're like a tiny hardware shop."
Vishal: "A cheap one. That's the point."

qa.q: Where does Vishal keep the tools?
qa.a: In the blue box, bottom shelf.

qa.q: How does Reena feel on opening the labelled tool box?
qa.a: Reena feels surprised and impressed, even teasing Vishal about being a tiny hardware shop.

qa.q: Which of Vishal's habits prevent costly repairs?
qa.a: Keeping tools in one place, using the correct screwdriver, and oiling hinges and the chain on the first Sunday of every month.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Reena's butter-knife method?
qa.a: Vishal sees it as the reason Reena's kitchen screws are chewed up, and gently points it out.

passage: I'm Ira, and when I set up my first flat in Pune at twenty-four, my friend Gurpreet gave me the most useful house-warming gift: a small toolbox. Screwdrivers of three sizes, pliers, a tape measure, a spirit level, a torch and a tiny oil can. I laughed. But I kept it in one place, under the sink. When the curtain rod sagged, I used the right screws and the level, not guesswork. Every two months, I oil the door hinges and check the pressure-cooker gasket. Last year my neighbour's cooker whistle jammed and it cost her a new cooker. Mine is still fine. Small care costs almost nothing. Big repairs cost a lot.

qa.q: Where does Ira keep the toolbox?
qa.a: Under the sink.

qa.q: How did Ira feel about the toolbox at first?
qa.a: Ira was amused, laughing at the gift before realising how useful it was.

qa.q: Which habits help Ira avoid costly repairs?
qa.a: Keeping the tools in one place, using the right tool for each job and checking hinges and the cooker gasket every two months.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel knowing the toolbox is still in use?
qa.a: Gurpreet would likely feel pleased and proud that the practical gift made such a difference.

grounding: A young adult describes keeping basic tools in one place, using the correct tool and doing small maintenance before things fail.

passage:
Workshop supervisor's note, community tailoring centre, Friday.
I want to record how Nandini, our newest trainer, runs her corner. Every sewing machine on her side has a small card listing the last oiling date. Her tools are hung on a board, each in its outline, so a missing pair of scissors is obvious at once. When a student tried to cut thick canvas with fabric scissors, Nandini stopped her gently and handed her the heavy shears. "Wrong tool, wrong result." In three months, not one of her machines has needed the repairman. The other side has called him four times. I have asked Nandini to show the other trainers her board on Monday.
Gargi

qa.q: How many times has the other side called the repairman?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: How did Nandini seem to feel when stopping the student?
qa.a: Nandini seemed calm and patient, gently handing over the right shears.

qa.q: Why has Nandini's corner avoided repairs?
qa.a: Regular oiling logged on cards, tools kept in one place on a board, and using the correct tool for each job prevent damage.

qa.q: How might the other trainers see Nandini's board when she shows it?
qa.a: The other trainers might feel curious and a little challenged, seeing a simple system that keeps machines working.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a trainer keeping tools in one place, using the right tool and doing small maintenance before things fail.

passage:
Sunday, 2 March
First Sunday of the month, so maintenance hour. Oiled the cycle chain and pumped both tyres. Pulled a horrible clump of hair out of the bathroom drain before it could block. Tightened the loose wardrobe hinge with the small cross-head screwdriver; took two minutes because I knew which drawer it lives in.
Yusuf came in holding a butter knife, trying to open the doorbell's battery cover. I handed him the tiny flat-head from the tool box instead. He laughed: "You have a screwdriver for everything." Then he told me that in his last flat he used pliers on a tap nut and cracked it, and the plumber took a whole morning to fix it.
One box, labelled, in the same cupboard. A handful of small jobs a month. I haven't had to call anyone out since we moved in, and I don't lie awake wondering what's about to break.
Santosh

qa.q: What was Yusuf using to try to open the doorbell's battery cover?
qa.a: A butter knife.

qa.a: Santosh feels calm and settled, not lying awake wondering what will break next.

qa.q: How does Yusuf react to Santosh's tool box?
qa.a: Yusuf is amused and a little impressed, laughing that Santosh has a screwdriver for everything, perhaps remembering the cracked tap with regret.
